_doc: Kho điểm ngữ pháp LexKite (P0.3 / P0-D, docs/CONTENT-WORLD-PLAN.md). 100% tự soạn: tên điểm, câu "Can use X to …" và ví dụ dấu hiệu cấp là của LexKite, không chép English Grammar Profile/sách (CONTENT-RULES §1). lessons = id bài trong web/js/grammar (bài cùng cấp gốc = "đã dạy"; bài lệch ±1 bậc = ôn/mở rộng). Điểm chưa dạy ở đúng cấp nằm trong hàng chờ content/pipeline/targets.json "Ngữ pháp – bài <cấp>".points. Kiểm: node scripts/content-qa/grammar-map-check.mjs. id điểm KHÔNG đổi/tái dùng.

points.name: be: am / is / are
points.can_do_en: Can use am, is and are to say who people are, where they are from and how they feel.
points.example: I'm Lan. She's from Hanoi. We're tired.

points.name: be: negatives and questions
points.can_do_en: Can make negatives and yes/no questions with be to check simple facts.
points.example: Is he your brother? No, he isn't.

points.name: present simple for routines
points.can_do_en: Can use the present simple with I/you/we/they to talk about daily habits.
points.example: I get up at six and walk to work.

points.name: present simple: he / she / it + -s
points.can_do_en: Can add -s/-es for he, she and it when describing someone's routine.
points.example: She works in a bank. He watches TV.

points.name: do / does in questions and negatives
points.can_do_en: Can ask and answer simple questions with do and does.
points.example: Do you like tea? She doesn't drive.

points.name: present continuous for now
points.can_do_en: Can use am/is/are + -ing to say what is happening at the moment of speaking.
points.example: I'm cooking dinner right now.

points.name: have / have got for possession
points.can_do_en: Can use have (got) to talk about family, pets and possessions.
points.example: I have two sisters. Have you got a car?

points.name: past of be: was / were
points.can_do_en: Can use was and were to talk about where one was and how things were.
points.example: We were at home yesterday. It was cold.

points.name: past simple of common regular verbs
points.can_do_en: Can talk about finished actions yesterday or last week with common -ed verbs.
points.example: I watched a film and played football.

points.name: be going to for simple plans
points.can_do_en: Can say what one is going to do this weekend.
points.example: I'm going to visit my grandma.

points.name: imperatives for instructions
points.can_do_en: Can give simple instructions and warnings with the base form.
points.example: Open the window. Don't touch that!

points.name: let's for suggestions
points.can_do_en: Can make a simple suggestion with let's.
points.example: Let's go to the park.

points.name: can / can't for ability
points.can_do_en: Can say what people can and cannot do.
points.example: I can swim, but I can't ski.

points.name: can for requests and permission
points.can_do_en: Can ask for things and permission politely with can.
points.example: Can I have a coffee, please? Can I sit here?

points.name: would like for wants and offers
points.can_do_en: Can order and offer politely with would like.
points.example: I'd like a sandwich. Would you like some water?

points.name: like / love / hate + -ing
points.can_do_en: Can say what activities one likes or dislikes doing.
points.example: I love dancing. He hates getting up early.

points.name: wh- question words
points.can_do_en: Can ask for information with what, where, when, who, how old and how much.
points.example: Where do you live? How much is it?

points.name: short answers
points.can_do_en: Can answer yes/no questions with short answers.
points.example: Are you hungry? Yes, I am.

points.name: regular plural nouns
points.can_do_en: Can form regular plurals with -s and -es.
points.example: two books, three boxes

points.name: common irregular plurals
points.can_do_en: Can use common irregular plurals such as people, children, men and women.
points.example: There are five people in my family.

points.name: a / an with singular nouns
points.can_do_en: Can use a and an before singular countable nouns.
points.example: a dog, an apple, an hour

points.name: the for things already known
points.can_do_en: Can use the for something both speakers know about.
points.example: The bus is late again.

points.name: this / that / these / those
points.can_do_en: Can point to near and far things with this, that, these and those.
points.example: This is my bag. Those are my keys.

points.name: some / any with food and drink
points.can_do_en: Can use some in positive sentences and any in questions and negatives.
points.example: We have some milk. Is there any bread?

points.name: how many / how much
points.can_do_en: Can ask about quantity with how many and how much.
points.example: How many apples do you need?

points.name: possessive 's
points.can_do_en: Can show who owns something with 's.
points.example: This is Tom's phone.

points.name: subject pronouns
points.can_do_en: Can use I, you, he, she, it, we and they correctly as subjects.
points.example: She is a teacher. They live in Paris.

points.name: object pronouns
points.can_do_en: Can use me, him, her, us and them after verbs and prepositions.
points.example: Call me later. I like them.

points.name: possessive adjectives
points.can_do_en: Can use my, your, his, her, our and their before nouns.
points.example: Their house is big.

points.name: adjective position
points.can_do_en: Can put an adjective before a noun or after be.
points.example: a red car; The car is red.

points.name: very / really with adjectives
points.can_do_en: Can make adjectives stronger with very and really.
points.example: It's very hot. She's really nice.

points.name: always / usually / sometimes / never
points.can_do_en: Can say how often one does something using frequency adverbs in the right place.
points.example: I usually walk. I'm never late.

points.name: at / on / in for time
points.can_do_en: Can use at with clock times, on with days and in with months and years.
points.example: at 7 o'clock, on Monday, in June

points.name: in / on / under / next to
points.can_do_en: Can describe where things are with simple prepositions of place.
points.example: The cat is under the table.

points.name: there is / there are
points.can_do_en: Can say what exists in a place with there is and there are.
points.example: There's a bank near my house.

points.name: and / but / or
points.can_do_en: Can join two simple ideas with and, but and or.
points.example: I like tea, but I don't like coffee.

points.name: because for reasons
points.can_do_en: Can give a simple reason with because.
points.example: I'm tired because I worked late.

points.name: subject–verb–object word order
points.can_do_en: Can build simple sentences in the order subject, verb, object, place, time.
points.example: I play tennis in the park on Sundays.

points.name: numbers, dates and clock times
points.can_do_en: Can say and write prices, dates and times.
points.example: It's half past three. My birthday is on 5 May.

points.name: capital letters and full stops
points.can_do_en: Can start sentences with a capital letter, end with a full stop and capitalise names.
points.example: My name is Ana. I live in Lima.

points.name: present simple for facts and timetables
points.can_do_en: Can use the present simple for general truths and fixed timetables.
points.example: Water boils at 100°C. The train leaves at 8.

points.name: present simple vs present continuous
points.can_do_en: Can choose between a habit and something happening now or around now.
points.example: I usually take the bus, but today I'm walking.

points.name: present continuous for temporary situations
points.can_do_en: Can describe temporary situations and changes in progress.
points.example: I'm staying with friends this month.

points.name: present continuous for arrangements
points.can_do_en: Can talk about fixed future arrangements with the present continuous.
points.example: We're meeting Ana on Friday.

points.name: past simple of irregular verbs
points.can_do_en: Can use common irregular past forms to tell what happened.
points.example: We went to the beach and ate fish.

points.name: past simple questions and negatives with did
points.can_do_en: Can ask and answer about the past using did and didn't.
points.example: Did you see Tom? No, I didn't.

points.name: past time expressions
points.can_do_en: Can place past events with ago, last, yesterday and in + year.
points.example: I moved here two years ago.

points.name: past continuous for background
points.can_do_en: Can set the scene of a story with the past continuous.
points.example: It was raining and people were hurrying home.

points.name: present perfect for experiences
points.can_do_en: Can talk about life experiences with have/has + past participle and ever/never.
points.example: Have you ever been to Japan? I've never tried sushi.

points.name: be going to for evidence-based predictions
points.can_do_en: Can predict something from present evidence with going to.
points.example: Look at those clouds – it's going to rain.

points.name: will for instant decisions and offers
points.can_do_en: Can use will for decisions made while speaking and for offers.
points.example: I'll carry that for you.

points.name: used to for past habits
points.can_do_en: Can contrast past habits and states with the present using used to.
points.example: I used to live in a village.

points.name: have to / must for obligation
points.can_do_en: Can say what is necessary with have to and must.
points.example: I have to work on Saturday.

points.name: don't have to vs mustn't
points.can_do_en: Can distinguish lack of obligation from prohibition.
points.example: You don't have to come. You mustn't smoke here.

points.name: should for advice
points.can_do_en: Can give and ask for advice with should.
points.example: You should see a doctor.

points.name: could for past ability
points.can_do_en: Can say what someone could or couldn't do in the past.
points.example: I could read when I was four.

points.name: might / may for possibility
points.can_do_en: Can express that something is possible with might and may.
points.example: I might go out tonight.

points.name: zero conditional
points.can_do_en: Can describe general results with if + present, present.
points.example: If you heat ice, it melts.

points.name: first conditional
points.can_do_en: Can talk about likely future results with if + present, will.
points.example: If it rains, we'll stay at home.

points.name: verb + to-infinitive (want, need, hope)
points.can_do_en: Can follow common verbs with to + base form.
points.example: I want to learn French.

points.name: to-infinitive of purpose
points.can_do_en: Can explain why one does something with to + verb.
points.example: I went to the shop to buy milk.

points.name: countable and uncountable nouns
points.can_do_en: Can recognise uncountable nouns such as advice, information and money.
points.example: Can you give me some information?

points.name: much / many / a lot of
points.can_do_en: Can talk about quantity with much, many and a lot of.
points.example: There isn't much time. We have a lot of homework.

points.name: a few / a little
points.can_do_en: Can talk about small quantities with a few and a little.
points.example: I have a few friends here. Add a little salt.

points.name: no article with general plurals and uncountables
points.can_do_en: Can leave out the article when talking about things in general.
points.example: Dogs are friendly. I like music.

points.name: a for first mention, the for second
points.can_do_en: Can switch from a to the once something has been mentioned.
points.example: I saw a film. The film was long.

points.name: common compound nouns
points.can_do_en: Can use noun + noun combinations such as bus stop and coffee cup.
points.example: Wait at the bus stop.

points.name: possessive pronouns
points.can_do_en: Can use mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs instead of a noun.
points.example: That bag isn't mine – it's hers.

points.name: reflexive pronouns (basic)
points.can_do_en: Can use myself, yourself etc. when subject and object are the same.
points.example: He hurt himself.

points.name: something / anyone / nobody
points.can_do_en: Can use indefinite pronouns in statements and questions.
points.example: Is anyone there? Nobody called.

points.name: one / ones to avoid repetition
points.can_do_en: Can replace a noun with one or ones.
points.example: I don't like the red shirt, but I like the blue one.

points.name: comparatives of short adjectives
points.can_do_en: Can compare two things with -er than.
points.example: My flat is smaller than yours.

points.name: more / less + long adjectives
points.can_do_en: Can compare with more and less before longer adjectives.
points.example: This film is more interesting.

points.name: superlatives
points.can_do_en: Can say which is the most or least in a group.
points.example: It's the tallest building in the city.

points.name: as … as for equality
points.can_do_en: Can say two things are equal or not with (not) as … as.
points.example: He's not as tall as his brother.

points.name: adverbs of manner
points.can_do_en: Can describe how someone does something with -ly adverbs and irregular forms.
points.example: She speaks slowly. He drives fast.

points.name: -ed vs -ing adjectives (basic)
points.can_do_en: Can distinguish how one feels from what causes the feeling.
points.example: I'm bored. The film is boring.

points.name: too and enough
points.can_do_en: Can say something is more or less than needed.
points.example: It's too expensive. I'm not old enough.

points.name: prepositions of movement
points.can_do_en: Can describe movement with into, out of, across, along and through.
points.example: Walk along the river and cross the bridge.

points.name: for / since / during / until
points.can_do_en: Can talk about time periods with common time prepositions.
points.example: I waited until six. It rained during the night.

points.name: subject vs object questions
points.can_do_en: Can ask who did something without do/did when who is the subject.
points.example: Who called you? Who did you call?

points.name: how + adjective/adverb questions
points.can_do_en: Can ask how long, how often, how far and how much.
points.example: How often do you go to the gym?

points.name: questions ending in a preposition
points.can_do_en: Can ask natural questions with the preposition at the end.
points.example: Who are you talking to?

points.name: when / before / after clauses
points.can_do_en: Can link two events in time with when, before and after.
points.example: After I finish work, I'll call you.

points.name: so for results
points.can_do_en: Can show a result with so.
points.example: It was late, so we took a taxi.

points.name: first / then / after that / finally
points.can_do_en: Can order events in a story or a process.
points.example: First, mix the flour. Then add the eggs.

points.name: it for weather, time and distance
points.can_do_en: Can use it as an empty subject.
points.example: It's raining. It's ten kilometres from here.

points.name: polite requests with could / would you mind
points.can_do_en: Can make polite requests with could you and would you mind + -ing.
points.example: Could you open the door? Would you mind waiting?

points.name: why don't we / how about
points.can_do_en: Can make and respond to suggestions with why don't we and how about + -ing.
points.example: How about going to the cinema?

points.name: -ed and -s endings: spelling and sound
points.can_do_en: Can spell -ed, -ing and -s forms and say -ed as /t/, /d/ or /ɪd/.
points.example: stopped /t/, played /d/, wanted /ɪd/

points.name: nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs
points.can_do_en: Can recognise the main parts of speech and the five basic sentence patterns.
points.example: S + V + O: She reads books.

points.name: question tags with be and do (basic)
points.can_do_en: Can check information with simple question tags.
points.example: It's cold, isn't it?

points.name: 's vs of
points.can_do_en: Can choose between 's for people and of for things.
points.example: my sister's car; the end of the film

points.name: common stative verbs
points.can_do_en: Can avoid -ing with verbs such as know, like and want.
points.example: I know the answer (not I'm knowing).

points.name: percentages, fractions and large numbers
points.can_do_en: Can read numbers, percentages and simple fractions aloud.
points.example: Half of the class; 25 per cent

points.name: present perfect with for / since
points.can_do_en: Can describe situations that started in the past and continue now.
points.example: I've lived here since 2019.

points.name: present perfect with just / already / yet
points.can_do_en: Can report recent actions and check progress.
points.example: Have you finished yet? I've just arrived.

points.name: present perfect vs past simple
points.can_do_en: Can choose between unfinished time and a finished past time.
points.example: I've seen it twice. I saw it last week.

points.name: present perfect continuous for duration and recent activity
points.can_do_en: Can stress how long an activity has been going on or explain present results.
points.example: I've been waiting for an hour. You look tired – have you been running?

points.name: past continuous interrupted by past simple
points.can_do_en: Can tell what was happening when something else happened.
points.example: I was cooking when the phone rang.

points.name: past perfect for earlier past
points.can_do_en: Can show that one past event happened before another.
points.example: When we arrived, the film had started.

points.name: past perfect continuous (introduction)
points.can_do_en: Can explain a past situation by an earlier ongoing activity.
points.example: She was tired because she had been working all day.

points.name: will vs going to vs present continuous
points.can_do_en: Can choose the right future form for predictions, plans and arrangements.
points.example: I'm flying on Monday. I think it will be fine.

points.name: present tense in future time clauses
points.can_do_en: Can use the present after when, as soon as and until for the future.
points.example: I'll call you when I get home.

points.name: used to vs would for past habits
points.can_do_en: Can use would for repeated past actions but not for past states.
points.example: Every summer we would swim in the lake.

points.name: be used to / get used to
points.can_do_en: Can talk about familiarity and adapting to something new.
points.example: I'm getting used to driving on the left.

points.name: stative vs dynamic meanings
points.can_do_en: Can use verbs like think and have with stative and dynamic meanings.
points.example: I think it's good. I'm thinking about it.

points.name: must vs have to
points.can_do_en: Can distinguish personal obligation from external rules.
points.example: I must call Mum. We have to wear a uniform.

points.name: should / ought to / had better
points.can_do_en: Can give advice and warnings with different strengths.
points.example: You'd better leave now or you'll miss the bus.

points.name: need to / don't need to / needn't
points.can_do_en: Can say what is and is not necessary.
points.example: You needn't bring anything.

points.name: be allowed to / could / can for permission
points.can_do_en: Can talk about rules now and in the past.
points.example: We weren't allowed to use phones at school.

points.name: be able to / manage to
points.can_do_en: Can talk about ability in tenses where can is not possible.
points.example: I haven't been able to sleep.

points.name: must / can't / might for present deduction
points.can_do_en: Can make logical guesses about the present.
points.example: She must be at home – the lights are on.

points.name: passive: present and past simple
points.can_do_en: Can describe processes and events when the doer is unknown or unimportant.
points.example: Paper is made from wood. The bridge was built in 1890.

points.name: passive with modals and perfect tenses
points.can_do_en: Can use the passive with will, can, must and the present perfect.
points.example: The results will be announced tomorrow.

points.name: passive with by + agent
points.can_do_en: Can add the doer with by when it is new or important.
points.example: The novel was written by a young teacher.

points.name: second conditional
points.can_do_en: Can talk about unreal or unlikely present and future situations.
points.example: If I had more money, I'd travel the world.

points.name: third conditional
points.can_do_en: Can imagine different past results and express regret.
points.example: If we'd left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train.

points.name: unless / in case / as long as
points.can_do_en: Can express conditions with unless, in case and as long as.
points.example: Take an umbrella in case it rains.

points.name: wish + past simple
points.can_do_en: Can express wishes about the present.
points.example: I wish I lived nearer the sea.

points.name: reported statements with tense backshift
points.can_do_en: Can report what someone said, changing tenses and pronouns.
points.example: She said she was tired.

points.name: reported questions
points.can_do_en: Can report questions with normal word order.
points.example: He asked me where I lived.

points.name: reported requests and commands
points.can_do_en: Can report instructions with tell/ask + object + to-infinitive.
points.example: She told us to wait outside.

points.name: say vs tell
points.can_do_en: Can choose say or tell in reported speech.
points.example: He told me the news. He said it was urgent.

points.name: gerund as subject and after prepositions
points.can_do_en: Can use -ing forms as nouns and after prepositions.
points.example: Swimming is good exercise. I'm interested in learning Spanish.

points.name: verbs + -ing vs to-infinitive
points.can_do_en: Can choose -ing or to after common verbs such as enjoy, decide and avoid.
points.example: I enjoy cooking. We decided to stay.

points.name: verb + object + to-infinitive
points.can_do_en: Can use want, ask and allow + object + to.
points.example: My boss asked me to write the report.

points.name: transitive and intransitive verbs
points.can_do_en: Can recognise which verbs take an object and which do not.
points.example: She arrived. He raised his hand.

points.name: linking verbs + adjective
points.can_do_en: Can use seem, look, become and feel + adjective.
points.example: You look tired. It became clear.

points.name: the with unique things, places and groups
points.can_do_en: Can use the with rivers, oceans, the sun, and groups such as the rich.
points.example: the Mekong, the internet, the elderly

points.name: each / every / all / both / either / neither
points.can_do_en: Can use common determiners to talk about all or none of a group.
points.example: Both options are good. Neither of them came.

points.name: few / little vs a few / a little
points.can_do_en: Can distinguish a small positive amount from almost none.
points.example: Few people came, so the room felt empty.

points.name: irregular and special plurals
points.can_do_en: Can use irregular plurals and nouns that are always plural.
points.example: criteria, phenomena; jeans, scissors

points.name: compound nouns and possessives with of
points.can_do_en: Can choose between noun + noun, 's and of.
points.example: a car door; the director's decision; the cost of living

points.name: reflexive vs each other
points.can_do_en: Can distinguish actions done to oneself from mutual actions.
points.example: They blamed themselves. They blamed each other.

points.name: order of adjectives
points.can_do_en: Can put several adjectives in a natural order.
points.example: a beautiful old wooden table

points.name: -ing / -ed adjectives and adjective + preposition
points.can_do_en: Can use emotion adjectives correctly and the preposition that follows.
points.example: I'm keen on hiking. She's worried about the exam.

points.name: much / a bit / far + comparative
points.can_do_en: Can make comparisons stronger or weaker.
points.example: It's much cheaper online.

points.name: the + comparative, the + comparative
points.can_do_en: Can describe two things changing together.
points.example: The more you practise, the easier it gets.

points.name: so / such … that
points.can_do_en: Can show a strong result with so and such.
points.example: It was such a good film that I watched it twice.

points.name: position of frequency and time adverbs
points.can_do_en: Can place adverbs of frequency and time naturally in a sentence.
points.example: I have never been there. I'll see you tomorrow.

points.name: prepositions in fixed phrases
points.can_do_en: Can use common preposition phrases such as on time, in time and by car.
points.example: We arrived just in time.

points.name: subject–verb agreement
points.can_do_en: Can make verbs agree with tricky subjects such as everyone, the news and a number of.
points.example: Everyone is here. The news is good.

points.name: defining relative clauses
points.can_do_en: Can identify people and things with who, which, that and where.
points.example: The woman who lives next door is a nurse.

points.name: non-defining relative clauses
points.can_do_en: Can add extra information with commas and who or which.
points.example: My brother, who lives in Berlin, is visiting.

points.name: omitting relative pronouns
points.can_do_en: Can leave out the object relative pronoun.
points.example: The book (that) I read was great.

points.name: although / even though / however
points.can_do_en: Can contrast ideas within and between sentences.
points.example: Although it was late, we kept working.

points.name: because / because of / since / as
points.can_do_en: Can give reasons with clauses and noun phrases.
points.example: The match was cancelled because of the rain.

points.name: so that / in order to
points.can_do_en: Can express purpose with so that and in order to.
points.example: I left early so that I could catch the bus.

points.name: while / as soon as / until / by the time
points.can_do_en: Can link events precisely with time conjunctions.
points.example: By the time we got there, it had closed.

points.name: question tags
points.can_do_en: Can form question tags for different tenses and use rising or falling intonation.
points.example: You've met her, haven't you?

points.name: indirect questions
points.can_do_en: Can ask politely with Could you tell me… and Do you know….
points.example: Do you know where the station is?

points.name: so do I / neither do I
points.can_do_en: Can agree briefly with positive and negative statements.
points.example: I'm hungry. – So am I.

points.name: simple, compound and complex sentences
points.can_do_en: Can recognise and combine sentence types for variety.
points.example: She was tired, but she finished because it was due.

points.name: too / enough + to-infinitive
points.can_do_en: Can link too and enough to a result.
points.example: It's too cold to swim.

points.name: common noun and adjective suffixes
points.can_do_en: Can build nouns and adjectives with -ment, -tion, -ful and -less.
points.example: develop → development; care → careless

points.name: negative prefixes
points.can_do_en: Can make opposites with un-, in-, im- and dis-.
points.example: possible → impossible

points.name: approximation and change in numbers
points.can_do_en: Can describe figures with about, nearly, over and doubled.
points.example: Sales nearly doubled to over 5,000.

points.name: in addition / also / as well as
points.can_do_en: Can add points in speech and writing with common linkers.
points.example: As well as being cheap, it's fast.

points.name: past perfect continuous
points.can_do_en: Can explain the cause of a past situation by a longer earlier activity.
points.example: The ground was wet because it had been raining all night.

points.name: future continuous
points.can_do_en: Can describe an action in progress at a future time and ask politely about plans.
points.example: This time tomorrow I'll be flying to Seoul. Will you be using the car?

points.name: future perfect
points.can_do_en: Can say what will be completed by a future time.
points.example: By 2030, the city will have doubled in size.

points.name: future in the past
points.can_do_en: Can report past expectations with was going to and would.
points.example: I was going to call you, but I forgot.

points.name: tense choice for describing data
points.can_do_en: Can choose past, present perfect and future forms when describing charts and forecasts.
points.example: Sales rose in 2010 and have remained stable since.

points.name: narrative tenses together
points.can_do_en: Can combine past simple, continuous and perfect forms in a story.
points.example: I had just sat down when someone knocked.

points.name: modal perfects for past deduction
points.can_do_en: Can speculate about the past with must have, might have and can't have.
points.example: She can't have seen us – she didn't wave.

points.name: should have / could have for criticism and regret
points.can_do_en: Can criticise past actions and talk about missed possibilities.
points.example: You should have told me earlier.

points.name: needn't have vs didn't need to
points.can_do_en: Can distinguish unnecessary actions that happened from those that didn't.
points.example: You needn't have bought flowers.

points.name: would rather / would prefer / had better
points.can_do_en: Can express preferences and strong advice with correct verb forms.
points.example: I'd rather stay in. I'd prefer you not to smoke.

points.name: it's time / it's high time + past
points.can_do_en: Can say something should already be happening.
points.example: It's high time we left.

points.name: impersonal passive reporting
points.can_do_en: Can report opinions formally with It is said that and is thought to.
points.example: The castle is said to be haunted.

points.name: causative have / get something done
points.can_do_en: Can say that someone else does a service for us.
points.example: I had my hair cut. We need to get the roof repaired.

points.name: passive infinitives and gerunds
points.can_do_en: Can use to be done and being done after verbs.
points.example: I hate being interrupted. It needs to be checked.

points.name: mixed conditionals
points.can_do_en: Can link a past condition to a present result and the reverse.
points.example: If I'd studied medicine, I'd be a doctor now.

points.name: wish / if only with past perfect and would
points.can_do_en: Can express regrets and complaints about the past and others' behaviour.
points.example: I wish I hadn't said that. I wish you'd stop talking.

points.name: provided / supposing / otherwise
points.can_do_en: Can express conditions with alternatives to if.
points.example: Provided that you pay on time, there's no fee.

points.name: as if / as though
points.can_do_en: Can describe how something appears with real and unreal comparisons.
points.example: He talks as if he knew everything.

points.name: reporting verbs and their patterns
points.can_do_en: Can report with verbs such as suggest, deny, admit and warn using the right pattern.
points.example: She denied taking the money. He suggested meeting earlier.

points.name: reported speech without backshift
points.can_do_en: Can keep the tense when the reported fact is still true.
points.example: He said the earth is round.

points.name: verbs with -ing or to and a change in meaning
points.can_do_en: Can use remember, stop, try and regret with different meanings.
points.example: I stopped to buy milk. I stopped buying milk.

points.name: phrasal verbs: separable and inseparable
points.can_do_en: Can place objects correctly with two- and three-part phrasal verbs.
points.example: Turn it off. I'm looking forward to it.

points.name: verbs and nouns + dependent prepositions
points.can_do_en: Can use the preposition that follows common verbs, adjectives and nouns.
points.example: depend on, an increase in, responsible for

points.name: articles with abstract and generic nouns
points.can_do_en: Can use articles with abstract nouns in general and specific senses.
points.example: Education is important. The education I received was excellent.

points.name: advanced quantity expressions
points.can_do_en: Can express quantity with a large proportion of, the majority of and a handful of.
points.example: The majority of respondents agreed.

points.name: extended noun phrases
points.can_do_en: Can pack information into noun phrases with several modifiers.
points.example: a rapidly growing online market

points.name: reference and substitution
points.can_do_en: Can avoid repetition with this, these, such, one, do so and so.
points.example: Many cities face this problem. Some have solved it.

points.name: ellipsis in speech and writing
points.can_do_en: Can leave out words that are clear from context.
points.example: I'd like to help, but I can't (help).

points.name: compound adjectives
points.can_do_en: Can form adjectives such as well-paid and time-consuming.
points.example: a ten-minute walk

points.name: the + adjective for groups and adjectives after nouns
points.can_do_en: Can use the young, the unemployed and adjectives placed after nouns.
points.example: the people involved; the elderly

points.name: advanced comparison
points.can_do_en: Can compare with twice as … as, nowhere near as and by far the.
points.example: It's by far the best option.

points.name: sentence and degree adverbs
points.can_do_en: Can comment on a whole sentence with adverbs such as clearly and surprisingly.
points.example: Surprisingly, the plan worked.

points.name: position of degree and focus adverbs
points.can_do_en: Can place only, even, quite and rather to change focus.
points.example: Only Tom knew the answer. Tom only knew one answer.

points.name: relative clauses with prepositions and whose / whom
points.can_do_en: Can use whose, whom and preposition + which in formal writing.
points.example: the town in which I grew up

points.name: reduced relative clauses
points.can_do_en: Can shorten relative clauses with -ing and -ed participles.
points.example: Students living on campus pay less.

points.name: participle clauses for time and reason
points.can_do_en: Can begin sentences with -ing or having + past participle.
points.example: Having finished the report, she went home.

points.name: noun clauses with that / what / whether
points.can_do_en: Can use clauses as subjects and objects.
points.example: What surprised me was the price. I doubt whether it'll work.

points.name: despite / in spite of / whereas / while
points.can_do_en: Can concede and contrast with prepositions and conjunctions.
points.example: Despite the rain, the event went ahead.

points.name: consequently / as a result / therefore / so as to
points.can_do_en: Can express cause, result and purpose formally.
points.example: Fuel prices rose; consequently, demand fell.

points.name: combining clauses for range
points.can_do_en: Can combine subordinate clauses to show a range of structures in writing.
points.example: While some argue that…, others believe that…

points.name: parallel structure
points.can_do_en: Can keep items in lists and comparisons in the same grammatical form.
points.example: She likes reading, writing and painting.

points.name: sentence transformations
points.can_do_en: Can rewrite sentences with the same meaning using different structures.
points.example: It's the first time I've seen it → I've never seen it before.

points.name: paraphrasing for academic tasks
points.can_do_en: Can paraphrase task prompts by changing word class and structure.
points.example: The number of tourists rose → There was a rise in tourist numbers.

points.name: commas, semicolons and colons
points.can_do_en: Can use commas after introductory phrases, semicolons and colons correctly.
points.example: However, the cost is high; the benefit is small.

points.name: cleft sentences (introduction)
points.can_do_en: Can emphasise one part of a sentence with It is/was … that.
points.example: It was the price that surprised me.

points.name: cohesive linkers in academic writing
points.can_do_en: Can link ideas with furthermore, on the other hand and in contrast.
points.example: On the other hand, costs are rising.

points.name: register and idiomatic expressions
points.can_do_en: Can choose formal or informal wording and use common idioms appropriately.
points.example: get the hang of it (informal) / become proficient (formal)

points.name: word families across word classes
points.can_do_en: Can change word class to fit a gap or a paraphrase.
points.example: economy, economic, economical, economically

points.name: language of trends and proportions
points.can_do_en: Can describe trends with nouns and verbs of change and modifiers.
points.example: a sharp rise; fell slightly; peaked at 40%

points.name: stative verbs in continuous forms for special meaning
points.can_do_en: Can use continuous forms of stative verbs for temporary behaviour.
points.example: You're being very kind today.

points.name: inversion after negative adverbials
points.can_do_en: Can emphasise with inversion after never, rarely, not only and little.
points.example: Not only did he apologise, but he also paid for the damage.

points.name: inversion after only + time expressions
points.can_do_en: Can use inversion after only then, only when and only after.
points.example: Only when I left did I realise my mistake.

points.name: inversion with so and such for emphasis
points.can_do_en: Can front so + adjective and such + be for dramatic effect.
points.example: So severe was the storm that schools closed.

points.name: wh-cleft sentences
points.can_do_en: Can focus on information with What … is/was.
points.example: What we need is a clear plan.

points.name: it-cleft for contrast and correction
points.can_do_en: Can correct or contrast with It was X, not Y, that….
points.example: It was the manager, not the staff, who decided.

points.name: fronting for emphasis and cohesion
points.can_do_en: Can move objects or complements to the front for focus.
points.example: This point I would strongly dispute.

points.name: inverted conditionals
points.can_do_en: Can use Should you…, Were it not for… and Had I known… in formal writing.
points.example: Had I known, I would have helped.

points.name: but for / without / otherwise
points.can_do_en: Can express conditions with prepositions and adverbs instead of if.
points.example: But for your help, we would have failed.

points.name: on condition that / assuming / in the event of
points.can_do_en: Can state precise conditions in formal contexts.
points.example: In the event of fire, use the stairs.

points.name: mandative subjunctive
points.can_do_en: Can use the base form after suggest, insist, recommend and it is essential that.
points.example: The committee recommends that he be dismissed.

points.name: were-subjunctive and formulaic subjunctives
points.can_do_en: Can use if I were, as it were and so be it appropriately.
points.example: If I were you, I'd accept.

points.name: hedging with modals and lexical verbs
points.can_do_en: Can soften claims with may, appear, tend and suggest.
points.example: The data appear to suggest a link.

points.name: hedging with adverbs and phrases
points.can_do_en: Can qualify claims with arguably, to some extent and in most cases.
points.example: This is, arguably, the main cause.

points.name: boosters and stance markers
points.can_do_en: Can strengthen claims with clearly, undoubtedly and it is evident that.
points.example: It is evident that further research is needed.

points.name: nominalisation
points.can_do_en: Can turn verbs and adjectives into nouns to write concisely and formally.
points.example: The government reduced taxes → The reduction of taxes…

points.name: complex noun phrases with post-modification
points.can_do_en: Can build long noun phrases with prepositional phrases and clauses.
points.example: the growing number of students choosing to study abroad

points.name: articles with abstract and institutional nouns
points.can_do_en: Can choose articles with nouns such as society, history and the economy.
points.example: in society; the history of science

points.name: advanced passive structures
points.can_do_en: Can use passives with get, with two objects and in perfect infinitives.
points.example: He is believed to have left the country.

points.name: impersonal it constructions
points.can_do_en: Can present ideas impersonally with It is widely accepted that.
points.example: It has been argued that…

points.name: reporting verbs that show stance
points.can_do_en: Can show attitude to a source with claim, acknowledge, contend and concede.
points.example: The author concedes that the sample was small.

points.name: nuanced modality
points.can_do_en: Can express subtle degrees of obligation and likelihood with be bound to, be supposed to and stand to.
points.example: Prices are bound to rise.

points.name: would for typical behaviour and criticism
points.can_do_en: Can criticise habitual behaviour with will/would and stress.
points.example: He WOULD say that, wouldn't he?

points.name: advanced participle clauses
points.can_do_en: Can use perfect and passive participle clauses, and absolute constructions.
points.example: The work completed, they went home. Weather permitting, we'll go.

points.name: relative clauses with quantifiers
points.can_do_en: Can use most of which, some of whom and none of which.
points.example: He has three sisters, all of whom are doctors.

points.name: sentential relative which
points.can_do_en: Can comment on a whole clause with which.
points.example: She arrived late, which annoyed everyone.

points.name: advanced concession
points.can_do_en: Can concede with however + adjective, much as and adjective + as/though.
points.example: Much as I admire him, I disagree. Strange as it seems, it's true.

points.name: whatever / however / no matter
points.can_do_en: Can express that something makes no difference.
points.example: However hard I try, I can't do it.

points.name: emphatic do and other emphasis devices
points.can_do_en: Can stress a contrast with do/does/did and emphatic words.
points.example: I did tell you – I'm sure I did.

points.name: varying sentence openings and length
points.can_do_en: Can vary sentence structure for rhythm and emphasis in extended writing.
points.example: Short sentence. Then a longer one that explains why.

points.name: advanced cohesion
points.can_do_en: Can use summary nouns such as this trend and these factors to link paragraphs.
points.example: This trend is likely to continue.

points.name: signalling nouns
points.can_do_en: Can organise argument with nouns such as aspect, issue and approach.
points.example: Another aspect of the issue is cost.

points.name: formal linkers and connectors
points.can_do_en: Can link ideas with nonetheless, hence, thereby and whereby.
points.example: Costs fell, thereby increasing profits.

points.name: future perfect continuous
points.can_do_en: Can describe the duration of an activity up to a future point.
points.example: By June, I'll have been working here for ten years.

points.name: past tenses for politeness and distance
points.can_do_en: Can use past forms to sound tentative.
points.example: I was wondering if you could help.

points.name: phrasal verbs vs formal verbs
points.can_do_en: Can choose between a phrasal verb and a formal single-word verb for register.
points.example: find out / discover; put off / postpone

points.name: advanced verb complementation
points.can_do_en: Can use complex patterns such as object + -ing, object + bare infinitive and it as object.
points.example: I find it hard to believe. I heard her leave.

points.name: advanced quantifiers and partitives
points.can_do_en: Can express quantity precisely with a fraction of, a great deal of and a wealth of.
points.example: a wealth of evidence

points.name: adjective + clause patterns
points.can_do_en: Can use adjective + that-clause and adjective + to-infinitive with subjects.
points.example: It is vital that everyone attends. She is sure to win.

points.name: comparison with progressive and proportional forms
points.can_do_en: Can use increasingly, ever more and in comparison with.
points.example: It is becoming ever more difficult.

points.name: ellipsis and substitution in formal writing
points.can_do_en: Can avoid repetition with do so, the former / the latter and so too.
points.example: The former is cheaper; the latter is faster.

points.name: punctuation for complex sentences
points.can_do_en: Can use dashes, parentheses and colons for emphasis and explanation.
points.example: The result – unexpected – changed everything.

points.name: idiomatic grammar and fixed expressions
points.can_do_en: Can use idioms and fixed grammatical expressions naturally in context.
points.example: It goes without saying that…

points.name: noun clauses in subject position and apposition
points.can_do_en: Can use the fact that, the idea that and whether-clauses as subjects.
points.example: The fact that he lied is irrelevant.

points.name: paraphrase with structural transformation
points.can_do_en: Can rewrite complex sentences using nominalisation, inversion and passives.
points.example: Because prices rose, demand fell → The rise in prices led to a fall in demand.

points.name: summarising reported speech
points.can_do_en: Can summarise what several speakers said using reporting verbs and nouns.
points.example: There was general agreement that…

points.name: unreal past forms
points.can_do_en: Can use would rather, suppose and as if with past forms for hypothetical meaning.
points.example: Suppose you lost your job – what would you do?

points.name: register control
points.can_do_en: Can shift register within a text, e.g. from formal report to informal summary.
points.example: In short, it didn't work.

points.name: parallelism in complex sentences
points.can_do_en: Can keep parallel structure in correlative pairs such as not only … but also.
points.example: The plan is both cheaper and faster.

points.name: full range of inversion patterns
points.can_do_en: Can use inversion after hardly, scarcely, no sooner, under no circumstances and on no account with ease.
points.example: No sooner had we sat down than the lights went out.

points.name: inversion after adverbials of place
points.can_do_en: Can invert subject and verb after place adverbials for literary effect.
points.example: Into the room walked a tall stranger.

points.name: inversion in comparisons
points.can_do_en: Can use inversion after as and than in formal comparisons.
points.example: She was very clever, as was her sister.

points.name: all cleft and pseudo-cleft types
points.can_do_en: Can use reversed wh-clefts and all-clefts for precise focus.
points.example: That is what I meant. All I want is some peace.

points.name: conditionals with modal and tense nuance
points.can_do_en: Can blend conditionals with modals and tenses to express fine distinctions.
points.example: If he should happen to call, tell him I'm out.

points.name: implied and elliptical conditionals
points.can_do_en: Can imply conditions without if.
points.example: Given more time, we could have finished. One more mistake and you're out.

points.name: formal subjunctive and fixed expressions
points.can_do_en: Can use subjunctive forms in legal and formal register, and fixed phrases like be that as it may.
points.example: Be that as it may, the rule stands.

points.name: subtle aspect contrasts
points.can_do_en: Can exploit aspect for nuance, e.g. tentative, emotional or annoyed meanings.
points.example: I've been meaning to call you. You're always losing your keys!

points.name: historic present and tense shifts in narrative
points.can_do_en: Can use the present for vivid past narration and headlines.
points.example: So I'm standing there, and this man walks up…

points.name: tense and modal for social distance
points.can_do_en: Can soften requests and refusals with layered past and modal forms.
points.example: I was just wondering whether you might possibly be able to…

points.name: full range of modal meanings
points.can_do_en: Can use modals for subtle epistemic and deontic meanings, including dare, shall and needs must.
points.example: How dare you! Shall I take that as a yes?

points.name: modal perfect continuous forms
points.can_do_en: Can speculate about past ongoing activities.
points.example: She must have been waiting for hours.

points.name: precise hedging and stance
points.can_do_en: Can calibrate certainty exactly, combining hedges and boosters.
points.example: It would seem, on balance, somewhat unlikely.

points.name: evaluative language and stance
points.can_do_en: Can signal evaluation subtly through grammar, e.g. tellingly, notably, it is striking that.
points.example: Tellingly, no one objected.

points.name: high-density nominal style
points.can_do_en: Can write and decode densely nominalised academic and legal prose.
points.example: The implementation of the recommendations of the review…

points.name: generic reference with articles
points.can_do_en: Can choose a/the/zero article for generic reference across registers.
points.example: The tiger is endangered. A tiger needs space. Tigers hunt alone.

points.name: articles with names and titles
points.can_do_en: Can handle articles with names, titles and brand names in all contexts.
points.example: the Smiths, a Picasso, Brexit

points.name: passive for stylistic and textual effect
points.can_do_en: Can use the passive to manage theme and information flow in a text.
points.example: These findings were confirmed by a later study.

points.name: free indirect speech
points.can_do_en: Can recognise and use free indirect speech in narrative.
points.example: She stopped. Was this really the end?

points.name: nuanced reporting
points.can_do_en: Can report with subtle stance using purport, maintain, allege and insinuate.
points.example: The letter purports to come from the minister.

points.name: literary participle and absolute clauses
points.can_do_en: Can use absolute clauses and dangling-participle avoidance in literary style.
points.example: His voice trembling, he began to speak.

points.name: literary relative structures
points.can_do_en: Can use whereby, wherein and the like in formal texts.
points.example: a system whereby users pay monthly

points.name: comparative correlatives and proportion
points.can_do_en: Can express proportion with the more … the less and in proportion to.
points.example: The higher the price, the lower the demand.

points.name: literary concession
points.can_do_en: Can concede with be it, try as I might and for all.
points.example: Try as I might, I couldn't open it. For all his talent, he failed.

points.name: advanced ellipsis
points.can_do_en: Can omit subjects, auxiliaries and whole clauses naturally in speech and writing.
points.example: Sounds good. Done that already.

points.name: end-weight and end-focus
points.can_do_en: Can order information so that heavy and new information comes last.
points.example: It is unclear whether the proposal will be accepted.

points.name: extraposition
points.can_do_en: Can move long subjects to the end with it and there.
points.example: It is surprising how few people voted.

points.name: marked word order for effect
points.can_do_en: Can use unusual word order in rhetoric and literature.
points.example: Strange it may seem, but true it is.

points.name: rhetorical patterns
points.can_do_en: Can use tricolon, antithesis and rhetorical questions for persuasion.
points.example: We came, we saw, we listened.

points.name: subtle cohesion across long texts
points.can_do_en: Can maintain cohesion through lexical chains, substitution and parallelism over many paragraphs.
points.example: The issue … this problem … such difficulties

points.name: metadiscourse
points.can_do_en: Can guide readers with frame markers and self-mentions appropriate to genre.
points.example: As noted above… In what follows, I argue…

points.name: irony and understatement through grammar
points.can_do_en: Can use litotes and ironic structures.
points.example: It was not the worst idea he'd ever had.

points.name: full register range
points.can_do_en: Can move between colloquial, neutral and highly formal grammar for effect.
points.example: Gonna / going to / intend to

points.name: conversion and creative word formation
points.can_do_en: Can use and understand nouns as verbs and new coinages.
points.example: to google something; to adult

points.name: rare and learned affixes
points.can_do_en: Can use affixes such as quasi-, pseudo-, -esque and -ism precisely.
points.example: quasi-official, Kafkaesque

points.name: subtle adjective and adverb choice
points.can_do_en: Can use intensifiers and downtoners with exact collocational fit.
points.example: utterly exhausted, faintly amused

points.name: comparisons with idiomatic structures
points.can_do_en: Can use comparison idioms and structures like no more … than and all the more.
points.example: He is no more a doctor than I am.

points.name: precise quantification and approximation
points.can_do_en: Can quantify with exactness or calculated vagueness.
points.example: in the region of, upwards of, a shade under

points.name: punctuation for style
points.can_do_en: Can use punctuation for rhythm and nuance, including the semicolon and em dash.
points.example: She hesitated; then — suddenly — she agreed.

points.name: idiomatic multi-word verbs
points.can_do_en: Can use idiomatic multi-word verbs and their nominal forms accurately.
points.example: a shake-up, a breakthrough; come up against

points.name: grammar of genres
points.can_do_en: Can adapt grammar to genres such as abstracts, legal clauses and headlines.
points.example: PM to visit Hanoi. The Lessee shall…

points.name: spoken grammar features
points.can_do_en: Can use heads, tails and vague language naturally in speech.
points.example: That film, it was amazing. It's nice, that.

points.name: avoiding structural ambiguity
points.can_do_en: Can detect and rewrite structurally ambiguous sentences.
points.example: Flying planes can be dangerous → Piloting planes…
